'Being alone with men' implies an interpersonal/assault-related trigger context that is not reflected in the trauma type or elsewhere in the profile, making it clinically incoherent here.

Avoidance of unfamiliar places due to inability to assess danger can occur in PTSD, but alongside the selected triggers it pulls toward an interpersonal/urban threat pattern rather than a natural-disaster pattern. This becomes problematic because the threat items are not meaningfully linked to the disaster-specific cues represented elsewhere.

vignette: Kai, a 46-year-old auditor from a coastal town in the Pacific, lost his wife in a tsunami that swept through their village five years ago. He had been at work that afternoon, checking spreadsheets, when the first tremor sent his colleagues running. By the time he reached the shoreline, the water had already receded and then surged back, carrying debris and bodies. He never found her. The memory now returns not as a coherent story but as a sensory assault: he can smell the salt and rotting vegetation, taste the grit of seawater on his tongue, and yet the whole event feels so extreme that he sometimes doubts it really happened—a detail he mentions with a hollow laugh, as if his own mind is playing tricks. When he feels happy or even mildly relaxed, that fleeting sense of ease instantly dissolves: the pleasure itself becomes a trigger. In those moments he notices the particular stillness in the air—unusual silence that makes him feel something dangerous is about to happen—and the memory of that afternoon rushes back, complete with the taste of brine. Happiness, for Kai, no longer feels safe; it is a prelude to loss. He has developed a quiet set of strategies to manage these intrusions. He avoids talking about the tsunami with anyone, because the words themselves seem to summon the smell and the helplessness. He also avoids relaxing deliberately: he keeps his evenings filled with tasks—reviewing client files, fixing small things around his apartment—because letting go of vigilance feels like inviting disaster. He smokes more now, a pack a day, though he tells himself it is just something to do with his hands. The smoking does calm him for a moment, but afterward he only feels more numb, more convinced that he cannot stop bad things from happening, and that awareness makes him scan for threats even more carefully. The world, he has come to believe, is a dangerous place, and his own helplessness is the core truth of it. His job as an auditor has become a refuge precisely because it requires him to inspect details over and over. But he now avoids going anywhere unfamiliar; he cannot assess the danger in a new building or a street he does not know, so he takes the same route to work every day. Delays, even small ones—a train that is two minutes late, a meeting that runs over—trigger a sharp spike of threat: he assumes something bad is happening, perhaps a disaster that he cannot see. When this memory intrudes, it brings with it a raw sense of immediate threat—his chest tightens, his pulse races, as if the wave is about to crash over him again. At night, waking in the dark, he lies still listening for a sound that does not come, and the silence terrifies him more than noise ever would. That fear loops back into the memory: he hears the quiet before the wave hit. Kai’s numbness has deepened over time. He tells his therapist that he feels dead inside, and he knows his avoidance of relaxation keeps him from ever testing whether safety is possible. The less he relaxes, the more his body stays in alarm, and the more his negative appraisals—the world is dangerous, I can’t stop bad things—are confirmed. When he does briefly let his guard down, for instance while enjoying a sunny afternoon on his balcony, the happiness itself becomes a trigger: he suddenly smells the ocean, tastes salt, and the memory overwhelms him, reinforcing his belief that pleasure is a trap. That cycle has narrowed his life to a tight corridor of work, home, and controlled routes. He came to therapy only after his supervisor mentioned that his avoidance of unfamiliar client sites was affecting his performance. What frightens Kai most is not the memory itself but the possibility that he will never trust a moment of peace again—and he is beginning to wonder if that suspicion is already true. This conviction makes him more likely to suddenly recall the tsunami unbidden, as though the memory itself is the only proof that his helplessness is real. Because he already believes he cannot stop disaster, ordinary delays like a two-minute-late train now feel like imminent warnings, turning neutral events into powerful triggers. This memory has made him hyper-attuned to any sensory match—so that the taste of brine or the smell of salt now instantly triggers a full trauma replay, turning otherwise harmless sensations into potent triggers. This constant busyness has backfired: any unexpected stillness—a few minutes of waiting for a delayed train or an unfilled gap in his schedule—now itself triggers a sharp sense of threat, as his mind interprets any pause as a sign that danger is approaching.
